entries.name: Weather that behaves like weather
entries.what: A joint temperature, wind and solar signal that persists the way real weather does — cold snaps last for days rather than flickering — with regional variation that still adds up to the national picture.

entries.name: Prices that come out of physics, not out of a distribution
entries.what: Demand is built from weather and buildings; supply is stacked in merit order; the price is what falls out. Nothing samples a price curve directly.

entries.name: Ten years of real settlement data, revealed in order
entries.what: Nearly a decade of actual half-hourly GB settlement records, released to the simulation in the order they happened, so nothing inside can see a day that has not arrived.

entries.name: Buildings with real thermal behaviour
entries.what: Each home is modelled as a physical fabric with heat loss and thermal mass, which is why a cold week shows up differently in a well-insulated flat and a draughty semi.

entries.name: Households with hidden lives
entries.what: Income, essential costs, life events — job loss, illness, a new child — and the choice between paying and heating. All of it hidden from the supplier, as it is in reality.

entries.name: Business customers that fail like businesses
entries.what: Sector shocks, insolvency and late payment behaviour that differ from a household's, because a struggling company does not miss a bill the way a struggling family does.

entries.name: The price cap as a real constraint
entries.what: Ofgem's cap binds what can be charged rather than sitting in a lookup table, and it changes within the year the way the real one does.

entries.name: The industry's own settlement timetable
entries.what: Volumes are not final on the day. They are trued up over months, on the real schedule.

entries.name: Banking and payment rails
entries.what: Direct Debit collection modelled end to end — the bank, the acquirer, and the ways a collection actually fails.

entries.name: Futures beyond the real record
entries.what: Worlds that run past the end of the real data, so the supplier can be tested against conditions that have not happened yet.

entries.name: Bills that add up
entries.what: Every line — unit rate, standing charge, VAT, the non-commodity costs — computed and checked to foot, with the arithmetic itself under a control that can fail.

entries.name: Estimated bills, and the correction when the read arrives
entries.what: Bills built on an estimate when no meter read exists, then rebilled against the truth when it turns up — including when a customer leaves mid-cycle.

entries.name: Three clocks kept straight
entries.what: What happened physically, what was billed, and what was settled are three different dates, and the supplier reconciles all three per bill rather than pretending they agree.

entries.name: Money matched to the right account
entries.what: A payment arrives against a party, an account and an agreement. Allocating it correctly — including when the amount is ambiguous — is its own machinery.

entries.name: Telling can't-pay from won't-pay
entries.what: The supplier infers, from payment behaviour alone, whether an arrears case is hardship or choice — and it is allowed to get this wrong, which is the point.

entries.name: Noticing a customer who has stopped heating their home
entries.what: A perfect payment record with collapsing consumption is a warning sign, not a good customer. The supplier detects it from the data it can actually see.

entries.name: Weather-normalised demand
entries.what: Working out how much of a change in consumption was the weather and how much was the customer — an inference, from observations, that can be wrong.

entries.name: A real set of books
entries.what: Double-entry ledger, management accounts, and one reconciled definition of revenue used on every surface that reports it.

entries.name: Hedging, and the margin it explains
entries.what: Forward cover bought against the book, and a year-over-year bridge that accounts for where the margin actually went.

entries.name: Its own regulatory obligations, tracked
entries.what: A register of what the licence requires, checked against what the supplier is doing, with the physical-harm duties treated as the serious ones.

entries.name: Carbon measured on three ledgers
entries.what: Customer, portfolio and grid carbon accounted separately — the measurement the whole premise rests on.

entries.name: A pricing engine
entries.what: Building a tariff forward from the cost stack — wholesale, losses, network, policy — rather than inheriting a price.

entries.name: The collections journey, end to end
entries.what: Missed payment, reminder, dunning ladder, arrangement, and the point where a debt is handed on.

entries.name: Settlement true-ups on the real timetable
entries.what: Following a volume from initial settlement through each reconciliation run, and taking the financial consequence each time it moves.

entries.name: Debt and cash flow modelled per home
entries.what: Provisioning built up home by home, with the rules for how a payment clears against old and new charges made explicit, and a debt trajectory per home so that beating the forecast is something a manager can actually be measured on.
entries.test: Does the predicted arrears trajectory match what truly happened, and how fast and how accurately was hardship told apart from choice?
entries.status: Waits on the order in which a payment clears old and new charges
waits_on: the order in which a payment clears old and new charges

entries.name: Spotting a household going cold
entries.what: Consumption falling below what the building's physics says the home needs in cold weather is not a thrifty customer; it is someone going without heat.
entries.test: How many are found and how many false alarms — and the false alarm that matters is an empty house mistaken for a cold occupant.

entries.name: Prepayment offered well rather than imposed
entries.what: Moving a customer who can pay but will not onto prepayment, screened for vulnerability first and designed with credit that carries them over a weekend.
entries.test: Bad debt by meter type, holding payment method and financial stress constant — and the share of cases the vulnerability screen stops.
entries.status: Waits on one consistent reading of who counts as vulnerable
waits_on: one consistent reading of who counts as vulnerable

entries.name: Budget billing from the home's own physics
entries.what: Forecasts from the building rather than from a national average profile, a monthly payment that is right from the first month, and a mode where the customer names the bill they want and is shown the levers that reach it.
entries.test: Forecast accuracy by house type against the truth, and what accurate, controllable bills do to bill shock, arrears onset and leaving.
entries.status: Waits on a first monthly payment sized to a seasonal year, the cash-flow shape a seasonal bill produces and whether a household acts on a prompt about its own bill
waits_on: a first monthly payment sized to a seasonal year
the cash-flow shape a seasonal bill produces
whether a household acts on a prompt about its own bill

entries.name: Not heating an empty house
entries.what: Reading occupancy from the meter's own signature — base load only, no evening peak, weekday regularity, gaps that look like holidays — and setting back the heating automatically, with anything sharper strictly opt-in.
entries.test: Detection accuracy and false alarms against the truth, never setting back on inference alone for anyone who might be vulnerable.
entries.status: Waits on when a home is genuinely occupied, half hour by half hour
waits_on: when a home is genuinely occupied, half hour by half hour

entries.name: The property as the customer, not the occupant
entries.what: A record of a home's energy physics that outlives whoever lives there: quotes prepared before anyone applies, sign-up at the meter rather than the person, and the final bill actually collected when they leave.
entries.test: Cost to onboard, accuracy of the first monthly payment, final bills collected, and whether the meter point is retained across a change of occupant.
entries.status: Waits on people moving home, and the shocks that come with it
waits_on: people moving home, and the shocks that come with it

entries.name: Comparison against genuinely similar homes
entries.what: Similar homes chosen by building physics rather than by postcode, so the comparison is fair rather than merely local.
entries.test: The change each nudge produces by segment, measured against what that same household would have done untouched.
entries.status: Waits on a cost comparison shaped to the customer rather than averaged
waits_on: a cost comparison shaped to the customer rather than averaged

entries.name: Targets and streaks on money, carbon and timing
entries.what: Goals and progress on all four of money, carbon, shifting load and efficiency — offered to those who want them, and deliberately not regressive, so the free steps score as richly as the ones that cost thousands.
entries.test: Behaviour that actually changed against behaviour merely reported differently, by segment — and whether the saving rebounds later.
entries.status: Waits on whether a household responds to a game, and whether the saving rebounds
waits_on: whether a household responds to a game, and whether the saving rebounds

entries.name: Buying energy against the homes actually supplied
entries.what: The shape of what the supplier buys forward derived from how its own homes respond to cold, region by region, instead of from an industry average profile.
entries.test: Volume risk and shape error measured on a deliberately cold practice book, and how the position survives a crisis year.
entries.status: Waits on published forward prices to test the buying against
waits_on: published forward prices to test the buying against

entries.name: Tariffs between fully fixed and fully variable
entries.what: A fixed price for part of the expected volume, with caps, floors and a weather-linked element, so stability is sold to those who value it at a price that reflects what it costs to provide.
entries.test: What the promise costs in a cold year, across the weather distribution and the home's own sensitivity to it — and whether customers understood what they bought.
entries.status: Waits on how much a household values a stable bill and weather drawn as a distribution rather than replayed
waits_on: how much a household values a stable bill
weather drawn as a distribution rather than replayed

entries.name: Automated buying inside a set risk limit
entries.what: Timing and shaping the energy purchase automatically, and using batteries and vehicles with permission — always inside a limit set by the board, never as a speculative position on the book.
entries.test: Value captured against the limit, with a 2021-style tail survivable by construction rather than by luck.
entries.status: Waits on a risk limit set by the board, which is the board's alone to set and published forward prices to test the buying against
waits_on: published forward prices to test the buying against

entries.name: Running cheaply enough that the saving is the product
entries.what: Operating at a fraction of the overhead the price ceiling allows for, so that most of the contribution per account survives to be shared.
entries.test: Cost per account measured honestly against what the market actually clears at.

entries.what: Solar, batteries, vehicles, insulation, flow temperature and timing, each costed from this home's own measured behaviour rather than from a brochure.
entries.test: Did the promised saving actually arrive — and how much of it was the advice rather than the household drifting there anyway?

scale.real_world: A real GB supplier serves hundreds of thousands to millions of homes.

gaps.title: The book is 154–224 customers
gaps.what: Everything on this page is true of a supplier with 154–224 accounts. A real GB supplier serves hundreds of thousands to millions of homes. Scale is the largest single gap between this and a real energy retailer, and nothing above will tell you that, because every item can be genuinely built at this size. The project's own feeds do not currently agree on the exact figure — 154 (accounts in the live customer feed), 224 (book size used by the break-even analysis) — and that disagreement is itself unreconciled.

gaps.title: Half-built, not absent
gaps.what: Listed above as coming next, which understates it: these exist and work in part, and are not finished. The price cap as a real constraint — Ofgem's cap binds what can be charged rather than sitting in a lookup table, and it change; Carbon measured on three ledgers — Customer, portfolio and grid carbon accounted separately — the measurement the whole premi.

plan.when: waiting on earlier work to finish first

gaps.title: Nothing here has ever spoken to a real counterparty
gaps.what: All 8 connections to the real industry are unbuilt, so every figure on this site comes from a simulated world. One specification has been read in earnest (DCC (DUIS service requests)); the rest rest on secondary research that says to verify it before building.

gaps.title: No claim on this page yet links to a record a reader could use
gaps.what: Every item marked as built should be traceable to what makes it so. The records exist, and they are written for whoever maintains this project -- internal identifiers, maturity levels, file paths -- so sending a reader to them would satisfy the letter of the request and teach nothing. 19 of 19 built capabilities have no published record at all, because the evidence pages are generated from the architecture diagram and it covers a fraction of the work. Rather than link to the machine's own notes, each claim below states in plain words what checks it. A record written for a reader is on the plan and is the next thing built here.

gaps.title: This page cannot tell you whether the simulation is right
gaps.what: It reports what has been built and how far, not whether the world it models behaves like the real one. That is a different question, it is measured elsewhere in this project against real market history, and the measurement publishes its own worst failures. A capability list is the wrong place to answer it -- but it is answered.
